classification.difficultyReason: Single additions or subtractions of integers, including negative operands.

questions.mappingNote: All 22 parts assess one integer addition or subtraction. Parts a, b, c, h, m and r operate directly with positive operands; d, g, i, k, o, s and u add a negative; e, f, j, l, n, p, q, t and v subtract a negative. The closest common classification is add-subtract-integers.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 introduces integers and addition. Page 2 defines subtraction through additive inverses and demonstrates integer addition and subtraction in Example 1, with number-line movements. Adding a negative becomes subtraction; subtracting a negative becomes addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Single additions or subtractions of integers, including negative operands.

classification.difficultyReason: Multi-term directed-number calculations include regrouping, additive inverses and nested negatives.

questions.mappingNote: All 24 parts directly assess addition and subtraction of integers. Parts u and v additionally require simplifying a double negative inside parentheses.
questions.methodNote: Use commutativity and associativity to regroup sums, cancel additive inverses, and replace subtraction of a negative with addition. Example 2 supplies the multi-term and nested-negative method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multi-term directed-number calculations include regrouping, additive inverses and nested negatives.

classification.difficultyReason: Select convenient factor pairs and reorder or regroup using the taught laws; even the four-factor products require only direct application.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and d pair 5 with 20; b pairs 25 with 8; c pairs 4 with 25; e forms two products of 100; f groups 3 with 6 and 40 with 50. All directly assess integer multiplication.
questions.methodNote: Use commutativity and associativity to reorder and group factors into convenient products, following Example 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate positive-integer products by grouping convenient factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires splitting factors and choosing efficient regroupings, including three-factor products.

questions.mappingNote: Every part explicitly assesses factor splitting followed by integer multiplication. Parts a–d use two factors; parts e–f extend the same taught method to three factors.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 establishes commutativity and associativity of multiplication. Page 5 Example 6 splits factors, rearranges and regroups them into efficient products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires splitting factors and choosing efficient regroupings, including three-factor products.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise repeated adjacent-pair sums and interpret alternating sums written with ellipses.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply adjacent pairing to explicit alternating sums. Parts c and d extend the same method to ellipses and require counting pairs; b retains the printed final term 18.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 groups adjacent positive and negative terms into pairs with identical sums, then adds the repeated pair sums.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise repeated adjacent-pair sums and interpret alternating sums written with ellipses.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise equal-sum pairs and determine the number of pairs in finite sums represented with ellipses.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) has 12 consecutive positive integers; (b) has 16 consecutive integers from 10 to 25; (c) has 15 consecutive positive even integers and an unpaired middle term; (d) has 20 consecutive positive odd integers. All four use Example 4's equal-sum pairing method.
questions.methodNote: Example 4, Method 1 uses commutativity and associativity to pair first and last terms into equal sums. Method 2 reverses the sum and adds corresponding terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise equal-sum pairs and determine the number of pairs in finite sums represented with ellipses.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalises the reversed-sum demonstration to an arbitrary positive integer n and justifies the resulting formula.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 generalises Example 4 from ten terms to n terms. The closest catalogue skill is proving results involving integers; the assessed result is a general consecutive-positive-integer sum.
questions.methodNote: Page 3, Example 4, Method 2 writes the sum in increasing and decreasing order, adds corresponding terms, and halves the total. Pages 1–2 establish the addition properties supporting rearrangement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises the reversed-sum demonstration to an arbitrary positive integer n and justifies the resulting formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalises a geometric counting pattern to a symbolic sum.

questions.mappingNote: The response generalises the supplied dot pattern into an expression, making pattern-to-equation the closest catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Addition permits regrouping by commutativity and associativity. The question supplies the geometric method: count the same dots as a rotated square.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises a geometric counting pattern to a symbolic sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that using every digit fixes the sum modulo 9, use this invariant to bound proximity to 1500, and construct a valid arrangement attaining the bound.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill is proving results involving integers: the solution establishes divisibility by 9 and constructs a total attaining the nearest possible value.
questions.methodNote: The inspected pages introduce integers, addition, commutativity and associativity. Grouping digits by place value extends that integer-addition reasoning; the question introduces the optimisation task.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a place-value construction and justification that no permitted sum is closer to the target.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalise the parity obstruction to classify n modulo 4, then establish sufficiency by discovering a construction that extends equal-sum partitions in blocks of four.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) constructs and checks equal sums; part (b) uses the parity of the total; part (c) proves the general integer condition and establishes sufficiency by balanced groups of four. Integer proof is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use integer addition, commutativity and associativity to regroup sums. The permanent example within question 11 introduces equal-sum partitioning.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises equal-sum partitions and requires an impossibility argument and justification of all possible positive integer values.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied iteration while preserving leading zeroes, recognise cycles versus fixed points, and compare starting values to investigate whether the eventual behaviour is shared.

questions.mappingNote: Repeated integer subtraction is the closest available skill. The assessed enrichment task is discovering cycles and fixed points, rather than learning a separate algebraic method.
questions.methodNote: Pages 1–2 introduce integers and integer addition/subtraction. Question 12 itself supplies the digit-rearrangement iteration; solutions apply that procedure directly and preserve leading zeroes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Investigates repeated digit rearrangement and subtraction to identify eventual cycles and fixed points.

classification.difficultyReason: Discover the unsignposted rewrite of each all-nines term as a power of ten minus one, then track the resulting borrowing pattern to obtain the digit sum.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires a justified general result about a structured integer sum; prove-results-integers is the closest available skill.
questions.methodNote: Use integer addition and subtraction, grouping terms and decimal place-value reasoning. Rewrite each all-nines term as a power of ten minus one, then perform the subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires generalising a decimal place-value pattern and analysing borrowing across a long integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct products of two to four integers using the same-sign rule.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess multiplication of directed integers; part h repeats the four-factor form demonstrated in Example 1(d).
questions.methodNote: Use the same-sign rule and evaluate successive products from left to right. Page 8 Example 1 demonstrates products of two, three and four factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct products of two to four integers using the same-sign rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguishes negative bases from external negative signs and evaluates combinations of powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–m apply repeated multiplication and signs of powers; d–e distinguish an external negative sign from a bracketed negative base. Parts n–v use the sequence demonstrated in page 9 Example 3: evaluate powers first, then perform the remaining operation.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines powers as repeated multiplication and Example 3 evaluates powers before addition or multiplication. Pages 7–8 establish product signs; page 10 confirms the same-sign rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguishes negative bases from external negative signs and evaluates combinations of powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate explicitly bracketed calculations and apply signed multiplication and subtraction, including subtracting negative results; the operation structure is supplied.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess explicitly grouped integer operations.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate bracketed calculations first, use the multiplication sign rule, then add or subtract directed numbers. Page 8 Example 2 supplies the two-step working model.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate explicitly grouped integer operations in two steps.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply signed division rules, with later parts requiring a bracketed signed multiplication first; no choice of strategy or interpretation is needed.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–i assess signed quotients; j–n add a preceding signed product.
questions.methodNote: Use the same-sign division rule; zero divided by a nonzero integer is zero. Evaluate bracketed products before division, as in page 10 Example 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply integer division sign rules, sometimes after a bracketed product.

classification.difficultyReason: Compute the supplied bracketed quantities and combine them using signed division, addition or subtraction; brackets determine the sequence throughout.

questions.mappingNote: Every part combines division with another grouped integer calculation.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate explicit brackets first, then apply signed arithmetic, following page 8 Example 2 and page 10 Example 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate grouped signed quotients and combine their results.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the fraction bar as grouping, evaluate numerator and denominator separately, and divide their signed results using the demonstrated format.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess grouped integer calculations in stacked fractions.
questions.methodNote: Use the vinculum to group numerator and denominator, evaluate each, then divide with the same-sign rule; page 11 Example 5 supplies this exact format.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate numerator and denominator independently before signed division.

classification.difficultyReason: Organise a search over three two-digit factors while enforcing six distinct digits, compare distances from 30000, and ensure the search excludes every closer valid product.

questions.mappingNote: Integer multiplication is the closest available skill; the additional demand is constrained optimization.
questions.methodNote: Use ordinary integer multiplication and a systematic search under the stated distinct-digit constraint; no special search shortcut is supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Search constrained two-digit products and establish which is nearest the target.

classification.difficultyReason: Iterate the demonstrated digit-square rule and classify each trajectory when it reaches 1 or a member of the supplied cycle; the terminal behaviours are already given.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the stated iterative rule to each of the first ten positive integers; pattern-from-expression is the closest catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: The embedded example defines the sum-of-digit-squares iteration, and the supplied cycle establishes the second terminal state.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Iterate a digit-square rule and identify the terminal state for ten inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Move beyond finding a small solution to proving uniqueness by bounding both smaller factorials by (z−1)! and showing their sum cannot reach z! for z>2.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is an integer uniqueness proof.
questions.methodNote: Use the factorial definition embedded in the question. Split into z=1, z=2 and z>2, then bound both factorials by (z-1)! as in the supplied teacher proof.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove uniqueness of a factorial equation using bounds and small cases.

classification.difficultyReason: Discover sum-preserving replacements that eliminate ones and reduce larger terms to twos and threes, then compare equal-sum groups to prove the proposed product is globally maximal.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is proving maximality of an integer product under a fixed sum.
questions.methodNote: Use integer products and sum-preserving replacements. Follow the teacher answer's even/odd splitting argument and comparison 3²>2³, while explicitly handling 1s and the equality at n=4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove a global maximum by replacing integer summands while preserving their sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct reduction of numerical fractions using common factors.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–p directly assesses reduction by a common factor; simplify-fractions is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 13 defines irreducible fractions and demonstrates dividing numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor in Example 1. Improper fractions are retained in fraction form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct reduction of numerical fractions using common factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Includes unrelated denominators, mixed numerals, negative results and three-term expressions.

questions.mappingNote: All 24 parts directly assess addition or subtraction of fractions; parts k–v also require interpreting mixed numerals. The printed unusual forms in m and o are retained as additive whole-number-plus-fraction notation, confirmed by the teacher answers.
questions.methodNote: Use a lowest common denominator, convert to equivalent fractions, combine numerators and simplify. Convert mixed numerals to improper fractions as in Example 4(b).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Includes unrelated denominators, mixed numerals, negative results and three-term expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Locate a midpoint by rewriting fractions with a common denominator and doubling it to obtain an integer midpoint numerator.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly applies Example 2's fraction midpoint method. Comparing and ordering fractions is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 rewrites the fractions with a common denominator, then doubles numerators and denominators when their difference is odd to locate the midpoint.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Locate a midpoint by rewriting fractions with a common denominator and doubling it to obtain an integer midpoint numerator.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a midpoint by converting fractions to a common denominator and scaling to obtain an integer midpoint numerator.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 directly applies Example 2's fraction-midpoint method to 7/8 and 8/9.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 converts both fractions to a common denominator, then doubles numerators and denominators when their numerator difference is odd to identify the midpoint.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a midpoint by converting fractions to a common denominator and scaling to obtain an integer midpoint numerator.

classification.difficultyReason: Extends the taught halfway-fraction method to three equal intervals using equivalent fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Finding equal intervals directly assesses equivalent fractions and fraction differences; add-subtract-fractions is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 Example 2 scales equivalent fractions to create equally spaced numerators. Page 15 teaches common denominators and fraction subtraction. Scaling the endpoints to denominator 72 extends these methods to three equal gaps.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extends the taught halfway-fraction method to three equal intervals using equivalent fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Orders three or four fractions with unrelated denominators using equivalence.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d each directly assess ordering fractions with different denominators; all solutions follow Example 3.
questions.methodNote: The inspected comparison procedure and Example 3 find the lowest common denominator, rewrite each fraction and compare numerators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Orders three or four fractions with unrelated denominators using equivalence.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires comparison through distance from one rather than the usual common-denominator method.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is comparing fractions. Rewriting each fraction as one minus a unit fraction respects the printed restriction.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 explains inequalities and order on the number line; page 15 teaches common-denominator comparison. This question expressly excludes that method, so compare the positive unit-fraction distances below one.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires comparison through distance from one rather than the usual common-denominator method.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires finding a fraction within strict bounds and establishing that its denominator is minimal.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is comparing fractions within an interval; denominator minimization extends that skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 explains strict inequalities; page 15 compares fractions by rewriting with a common denominator. Test positive denominators in increasing order, then verify the successful fraction using equivalent fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires finding a fraction within strict bounds and establishing that its denominator is minimal.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a unit-fraction decomposition, then maximise a sum strictly below one by bounding alternative denominator cases and selecting the smallest permissible final denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) finds three ordered unit fractions summing to one. Part (b) compares bounds for denominator cases and finds the greatest sum below one. Addition of fractions is the closest catalogue skill, with comparison as a secondary skill.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions, common denominators and exact numerator arithmetic; compare exact sums. The constrained unit-fraction search extends the taught addition and comparison methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Finds ordered unit-fraction denominators and establishes a maximum under a strict bound.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires combining three pairwise products to determine a positive variable before evaluating a reciprocal sum.

questions.mappingNote: The principal reasoning combines pairwise products to obtain a square and selects its positive root. The final reciprocal sum uses the taught common-denominator method.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13 and 15–16 teach equivalent fractions, reduction and addition using a common denominator. The supplied teaching pages do not demonstrate determining positive variables from pairwise products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires combining three pairwise products to determine a positive variable before evaluating a reciprocal sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct an integer sum using each of ten distinct numbers exactly once.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires constructing and verifying a sum of fractions that is an integer; addition of fractions is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions, rewrite with a common denominator, add numerators and simplify, as taught on page 15.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an integer sum using each of ten distinct numbers exactly once.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires recognising useful groups in a sum of thirteen fractions without a calculator.

questions.mappingNote: Adding and simplifying fractions is directly assessed; strategic regrouping supplies the enrichment difficulty.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions, common denominators, addition of numerators and reduction to lowest terms. Apply the question's hint by grouping related denominators first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires recognising useful groups in a sum of thirteen fractions without a calculator.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalises a numerical comparison by combining algebraic fractions and proving positivity.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) directly applies the fraction-comparison method. Part (b) extends common-denominator subtraction to pronumeral denominators and uses the stated condition to establish positivity; this is the most advanced assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 teaches common denominators, equivalent fractions, comparison of numerators, and subtraction followed by simplification.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises a numerical comparison by combining algebraic fractions and proving positivity.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalises a numerical comparison by combining three algebraic fractions and proving positivity for n > 1.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) adds two numerical fractions then compares with a third using a common denominator. Part (b) extends the same method to pronumeral denominators and establishes positivity using n > 1; operating with algebraic fractions is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions and common denominators. Page 15 teaches comparison by equal denominators and comparison of numerators, and addition/subtraction by combining numerators then simplifying. Page 14 supplies the interpretation of inequalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises a numerical comparison by combining three algebraic fractions and proving positivity for n > 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove exhaustive four-term coverage through denominator bounds and a finite factor-pair or bounded search, then use the supplied splitting identity recursively while preserving distinct denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Integer-denominator existence, uniqueness and exhaustive enumeration are the most advanced assessed tasks; prove-results-integers is the closest catalogue skill. Factor-pair enumeration completes the requested 'all ways' argument in (c).
questions.methodNote: Equivalent fractions, common denominators, fraction addition and comparison support the bounds and identities. Question 16(d) supplies the unit-fraction splitting identity used in (e) and (f).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires exhaustive enumeration, uniqueness arguments and a construction preserving distinct natural-number denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the absence of exact change into restrictions on coin counts and mixed subsets, derive a global upper bound, and verify an attaining collection has no subset worth one frac.

questions.mappingNote: The principal task is a fraction quantity problem; its maximum and subset restriction require additional integer reasoning.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions and a common denominator to add coin values and compare possible totals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a maximum subject to restrictions on every possible subset of coins.

classification.difficultyReason: Turn the supplied triangle sum rule into subtraction recurrences, generalise a diagonal pattern algebraically, and extend it to the third and fourth diagonals using neighbouring-row formulas.

questions.mappingNote: The question progresses from numerical patterns to general diagonal formulas and proofs.
questions.methodNote: Apply the supplied harmonic-triangle sum rule using common-denominator fraction subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalise diagonal fractions and justify formulas using the triangle's recurrence.

classification.difficultyReason: Design an exhaustive digit search across possible deletion positions, test equivalence rather than ordinary cancellation, and account for all nonzero two-digit proper fractions satisfying the property.

questions.mappingNote: Simplifying fractions is the closest catalogue skill; the task adds systematic digit enumeration rather than ordinary factor cancellation.
questions.methodNote: Use fraction equivalence to verify digit deletion; the supplied example is retained as permanent question content.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find all two-digit fractions satisfying a misleading digit-deletion equality and establish completeness.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions, cancel common factors across up to three factors, and multiply using the explicitly taught procedure.

questions.mappingNote: All eighteen parts directly assess multiplication of fractions; mixed-number conversion is preparatory.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 multiplication steps and Example 1, continued on page 19, convert mixed numbers to improper fractions, cancel common factors, then multiply.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct products of fractions, whole numbers and mixed numbers, including three factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert mixed numbers where needed, reciprocate the divisor, and simplify the resulting product; each part directly follows the taught division method.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses division of fractions or mixed numbers using the explicitly taught reciprocal method.
questions.methodNote: Page 19 division steps and Example 2 change division to multiplication, invert the second fraction, cancel and multiply; mixed numbers are converted first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct division using reciprocals, with mixed-number conversion in the final four parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Nested fraction notation must be interpreted as division before cancellation.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts are numerical compound fractions, matching the catalogue skill directly.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 Preferred Notation and Example 3 treat a horizontal fraction bar as division and multiply by the denominator's reciprocal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Nested fraction notation must be interpreted as division before cancellation.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines bracketed addition or subtraction with fraction multiplication or division.

questions.mappingNote: Each part combines fraction operations; multiplication or division is directly assessed alongside addition or subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Page 19 Example 2(c) evaluates brackets first; page 20 Preferred Notation omits multiplication symbols. Use common denominators, reciprocal division and cancellation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines bracketed addition or subtraction with fraction multiplication or division.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate compound fractions by calculating their numerators and denominators before dividing.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5(a–j) applies the taught division method to compound fractions. Addition and subtraction inside each numerator or denominator use common denominators; parts f and j also require multiplication before subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Calculate grouped expressions first, convert division to multiplication by the reciprocal, cancel common factors and multiply. Page 19 Example 2(c) explicitly evaluates brackets before division.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate compound fractions by calculating their numerators and denominators before dividing.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate successive nested denominators using exact fraction addition and division.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 applies these fraction operations repeatedly to nested denominators. Simplifying compound fractions is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: The supplied teaching pages demonstrate simplifying before multiplying, converting division to multiplication by the reciprocal, and evaluating brackets first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate successive nested denominators using exact fraction addition and division.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of fractions before adding, subtracting or multiplying, then simplify exactly.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess powers followed by fraction operations. Order of operations with indices is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate powers as repeated multiplication. Use common denominators for addition and subtraction; cancel common factors before multiplying, as demonstrated on pages 18–19.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of fractions before adding, subtracting or multiplying, then simplify exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the missing multiplicand as the given product divided by three-fifths, then apply the taught reciprocal method and simplify.

questions.mappingNote: The unknown factor is found by dividing the supplied product by the supplied multiplier, directly applying the fraction-division method on page 19.
questions.methodNote: Change division to multiplication, invert the second fraction, cancel common factors, then multiply the remaining numerators and denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise division as the inverse of multiplication, then divide and simplify fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires reversing a stated division before multiplying and simplifying fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 reverses fraction division to recover the original number, then uses the taught cancellation and multiplication method.
questions.methodNote: The supplied teaching pages demonstrate cancelling common factors before multiplying and dividing by multiplying by the reciprocal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires reversing a stated division before multiplying and simplifying fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine fractions with different denominators, then divide their sum by the number of values.

questions.mappingNote: Finding the average requires division of a fraction by 3, making multiplication and division of fractions the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use a common denominator for the sum; change division to multiplication by the reciprocal and simplify, following the fraction-division steps on page 19.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine fractions with different denominators, then divide their sum by the number of values.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify five fractional factors and cancel common factors before multiplying.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed operation is multiplication of fractions; addition within each bracket is preparatory.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the brackets, then cancel common numerator and denominator factors before multiplying, following the multiplication guidance and Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify five fractional factors and cancel common factors before multiplying.

classification.difficultyReason: Add fractions with different denominators, then take the reciprocal to find the unknown.

questions.mappingNote: The unknown occurs in one algebraic fraction; solving it directly assesses the selected equation skill, supported by fraction addition and reciprocals.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions with a common denominator, then invert the fraction, consistent with the numerator-and-denominator inversion taught in the division instructions on page 19.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add fractions with different denominators, then take the reciprocal to find the unknown.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct partners from a defining relationship and justify existence and uniqueness for rational numbers.

questions.mappingNote: The four numerical responses use the defining sum-product equation, fraction division and direct checks. Part (b) generalises the same equation to establish the exceptional value and uniqueness.
questions.methodNote: Pages 18–19 teach common-factor cancellation, conversion to improper fractions, and division by multiplying by the reciprocal. Question 13 supplies its own perfect-partner definition and numerical demonstration.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct partners from a defining relationship and justify existence and uniqueness for rational numbers.

existingTransferReview.note: Decision 2 (James, 11 November 2026): published on the recorded review covering each question's current content; no new model review.

bankProjection.note: Source-confirmed category headings are omitted only from bank prompts and presentation. Explicit equivalent fraction notation repairs satisfy bank validation. Source booklet content and all questions are retained.
